source.title: Overparameterized Linear Regression Under Adversarial Attacks

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own standard prediction-risk results as feature dimension changes in linear regression and random Fourier feature regression, conceptually testing double descent beyond deep networks.
record.gate_note: Included results on ordinary prediction risk as model size changes. The paper's adversarial-risk curves and its discussion of performance as training-set size changes concern adversarial risk, not the ordinary test-risk versions here; cited results from other work were not extracted.
record.test_reason: Mostly an adversarial-robustness paper that uses double descent as background. It does report its own ordinary test-risk curves against features/samples in linear models. These are δ=0 simulations in Fig. 3 that match the Hastie et al. asymptotics, the latent-model standard risk in Fig. 1 and Fig. S.11(b), and a random Fourier feature sweep on the diabetes data in Fig. S.1. Together they bear on V4 outside deep networks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the paper does not present ordinary-risk double descent as its own finding. It takes known results (Hastie et al.) and shows the ℓp-adversarial risk is 1–2 times (risk + δ²‖β‖q²). From this it argues ℓ2-adversarial risk can show double descent, while ℓ∞-adversarial risk can blow up with more features, depending on input scaling. Adversarial training and lasso can prevent this.
record.recipe_differences: Studies linear regression, including minimum-norm estimators and random Fourier features, with random-matrix analysis and adversarial-risk experiments rather than reproducing deep-network size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The ordinary isotropic prediction-risk behavior differs with the signal/noise condition: for r² < σ², the overparameterized risk decreases monotonically; for r² > σ², it has a local minimum. Adversarial results elsewhere in the study also vary with attack norm and input scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: The ℓ2-adversarial risk shows a double-descent curve, while the ℓ∞-adversarial risk can grow without bound as features are added, even as test error goes to zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent in adversarial risk depends on the attack norm and on input scaling.

record.problems: The diabetes random Fourier feature result is presented only as a plot, with 10 experiments and no numerical test-error values in the text. The theoretical results apply under stated linear-model and feature-distribution assumptions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional ordinary-risk results were left out. Adversarial-risk plots and results were excluded because they do not measure the ordinary test-risk behavior named by the tested version.

untested.parts: Sample-size effects are discussed only for adversarial risk.
Noise and regularization effects on ordinary risk are not analysed as such. Ridge and lasso standard-risk curves (Fig. S.11b) are not discussed in the text.

missing.what: Standard (δ=0) risk of the latent-space model decreasing continually in the overparameterized region and beating the underparameterized region
Own δ=0 simulation results matching the isotropic asymptotics
Equicorrelated-feature standard risk (δ=0 curve and Lemma 14)
Standard risk under ridge, lasso and adversarial training against m/n (could bear on regularization removing the peak)

record.verdict_notes: R1 and R2 rest on a cited theorem; only the δ=0 simulations, Fig. 1 and Fig. S.1 are the study's own evidence. The Lemma 4 peak term σ²/(γ−1) shows the divergence is noise-driven, which bears on V6, but it is cited rather than tested. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Risk over training epochs is not measured.
The study does not test whether increasing training sample size raises ordinary test error near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests feature-size sweeps in linear regression and a random Fourier feature model, not all model classes or whether the phenomenon subsumes every classical U-shaped curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study does not test whether noise drives the peak, whether peaks split into multiple descents, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak in ordinary test risk.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective parameter count to test whether double descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: minimum-norm linear regression with isotropic features
rows.size_stated: m features; dimension ratio γ = m/n
rows.operation_detail: Asymptotic ordinary prediction risk as the number of features varies relative to training-set size.
rows.value: As m,n → ∞ with m/n → γ, almost surely: σ²γ/(1−γ) for γ < 1; r²(1−1/γ) + σ²/(γ−1) for γ > 1. The text describes a local minimum in the overparameterized region.
rows.note: The reported risk diverges at the interpolation ratio when σ² > 0, then decreases beyond it before approaching the null risk from below.
rows.check: The value is Lemma 4, a cited asymptotic from Hastie et al. The study's own evidence is the δ=0 simulations in Fig. 3 (n=300, 10 runs), which the row should cite. The value string drops the +σ² term. The text also says the overparameterized risk is never better than the underparameterized one, and that risk rises after the local minimum. So the second descent is incomplete rather than fully observed.

rows.subject: minimum-norm linear regression with isotropic features
rows.size_stated: m features; dimension ratio γ = m/n
rows.operation_detail: Asymptotic ordinary prediction risk as the number of features varies relative to training-set size.
rows.value: As m,n → ∞ with m/n → γ, almost surely: σ²γ/(1−γ) for γ < 1; r²(1−1/γ) + σ²/(γ−1) for γ > 1. The text states that in the overparameterized region the risk decreases monotonically toward the null risk from above.
rows.note: This is an explicitly reported signal-to-noise condition under which risk improves monotonically in the overparameterized region.
rows.check: Cited asymptotic (Hastie et al.), illustrated in Fig. S.2(a). For r²<σ², risk falls after the peak but approaches the null risk from above. It never beats the null estimator, so the descent is only partial.

rows.subject: random Fourier feature regression model (linear-in-parameters, one-layer readout)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep the number of random Fourier features and report test mean-square error.

conditions.value: diabetes dataset; 442 patients, 300 used for training and the remainder for testing

rows.note: The appendix describes this figure as an illustration of double descent; plotted test MSE values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: The study's own experiment, readable only from the figure. The appendix describes it as an illustration of double descent in test MSE.

relationships.condition: Random Fourier features on the diabetes data; latent-space linear model
relationships.reason: R3 shows test MSE falling again past m=n. The text says latent-model standard risk continually decreases when overparameterized and beats the underparameterized region (Fig. 1, not in rows).
relationships.display_finding: Diabetes test MSE declined again past m=n, while latent-model standard risk decreased throughout overparameterization and beat the underparameterized regime.

relationships.reason: For r²>σ², overparameterized risk has a local minimum then rises, and is never better than the underparameterized minimum (R1). For r²<σ², it stays above the null risk (R2).
relationships.display_finding: For r²>σ², overparameterized risk reached a local minimum before rising and never beat the underparameterized minimum; for r²<σ², it remained above null risk.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
